basis: New mission, no workbook source; authored per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md. Facts and sources: NHI single-payer system began 1995, near-universal coverage, run by 衛福部中央健康保險署 (NHI Administration). Premium rate held at 5.17% since 2021, confirmed unchanged for 2025 and 2026 by the NHI committee (全民健康保險會, Nov 2024 meeting; UHO/HakkaNews Nov 2025 coverage), vs South Korea ~7% and Japan ~10%. Safety reserve (安全準備金) projected at ~2.1-2.2 months of benefit payments at end of 2025 per the Nov 2024 committee meeting (mohw.gov.tw cp-4624 series; wantrich.chinatimes.com 2026-05-09 coverage of Minister 石崇良). Taiwan crossed 20% 65+ population in 2025 (467.3万, 20.06%), officially a "super-aged society" per Ministry of Interior data (CNA 2026-01-09 reports; 14% threshold reached 2018). Old-age dependency ratio ~27 per 100 working-age residents in 2025 (moi.gov.tw statistical bulletin); longer-range ~2 working-age adults per elderly by 2040 cited via globaltaiwan.org/Brookings commentary — kept general, not stated as a precise official figure. National medical-expenditure long-range projection (~NT$1.3 trillion circa 2020 rising several-fold by mid-century) from a government science-policy forecast (cited via ctee.com.tw), kept in general terms per playbook guidance since the multiple is approximate. Health spending ~6.6-6.9% of GDP vs OECD ~9.7%, Japan ~10.6%, South Korea ~8.4%, US ~17% (mohw.gov.tw national health expenditure report; twreporter.org OECD comparison piece). NHI total annual budget passed NT$800 billion circa 2022 (mohw.gov.tw cp-5020-63299). Health Bank (健康存摺) ~12 million users, several hundred million data views, now linking Google/Apple/Garmin wearable data via SDK (mohw.gov.tw cp-16-79026 Google/NHI Administration release). "AI-on-DM" partnership with Google and National Health Research Institutes announced 2024 to predict type-2 diabetes complications, planned to extend to other chronic diseases (blog.google zh-tw 2024 Cloud Summit Taipei release; taiwan-healthcare.org coverage; cohesiondata.com news). Family-medicine/大家醫計畫 integrated-care clinics described only in general terms ("thousands of clinics") since an exact current count was not confirmed. No partisan cross-strait framing used. Register and structure per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md; calibration matched to content/authored/levels/sdg13-1.*.json.

slides.1: You carry a small green card in your wallet. It pays for your doctor, your medicine and your dentist. Today I want to ask: can Taiwan keep paying for it?
slides.2: SDG 3 has one clear goal: good health and well-being for everyone. It means care for the body and the mind, at every age, in every country. Taiwan takes this seriously.
slides.3: Taiwan built one big health insurance plan in 1995. We call it NHI. Almost every person here has this card, and doctors around the world still study how it works.
slides.4: In 2025, Taiwan passed a big number. One in five people is now 65 or older. This is called a super-aged society, and it changes how much health care we need.
slides.5: More older people means more visits to the hospital. Medical costs are rising fast every single year. Experts say the bill could grow much bigger before 2050.
slides.6: Here is the strange part. Health insurance rates stayed the same after 2021. But the safety fund gets smaller every single year, and nobody wants to raise the price.
slides.7: NHI started in 1995. Now it covers almost everyone on this island. That is a real achievement, and very few countries do this so well.
slides.8: Taiwan spends less money on health care than Japan, Korea or the United States. Still, almost everyone here gets care. Nobody pays huge bills to see a doctor.
slides.9: Taiwan built a digital health record called the Health Bank. Millions of people use it, and it can now connect to your smartwatch too.
slides.10: Leaders face a hard choice. They can raise the health insurance rate, or they can collect it from more kinds of income. Both choices make someone angry.
slides.11: One good idea is to catch sickness early. Family doctors can check on patients before they get very sick. This costs less than treating a bad disease later.
slides.12: Doctors are now testing smart computer programs. These programs study health data and try to guess who might get sick. The goal is to act early, not late.
slides.13: Here is the risk. If the safety fund drops too low, the law says the government must act fast. That could mean higher costs or smaller benefits for us.
slides.14: So who pays if rates go up? Young workers pay a share of every paycheck. A higher rate would hit new graduates hardest, right when they start their first job.
slides.15: Some people say: just copy Japan's rate. But a bigger number alone will not fix the real problem. Taiwan also has to change how care works, not just its price.
slides.16: Time is short. Many older workers are retiring right now, so fewer people pay into the system. Taiwan must decide soon, before the choice gets made for us.
slides.17: Let's sum this up. NHI is one of Taiwan's best ideas. But it is also under real pressure, and that pressure grows bigger every year.
slides.18: This is not just a government problem. It is your card, your future premium, and your parents' care. You already have a stake in how this story ends.
slides.19: Students like you can help. You can study the data, build better tools, or simply learn the facts and share them. This problem needs sharp minds, not louder complaints.
slides.20: Taiwan built something special. Almost everyone here gets care, and the price stays fair. What we choose now will shape this system for a long time.
